questions.scenario: The board wants 'AI' for three ideas: reading supplier invoices, a weekly demand forecast per store, and help drafting emails in Outlook.
options: All three in one Foundry agent
Document Intelligence for invoices, Azure Machine Learning for the forecast, Microsoft 365 Copilot for email drafting
Azure OpenAI for all three, because it is the most capable
Copilot Studio for invoices, Document Intelligence for forecasts, Azure OpenAI for email
questions.explanation: Invoices are a prebuilt perception task, forecasting from your own history is classic machine learning, and email drafting is a finished product to buy. Naming the kind first picks the service, the price model and the risk.

questions.scenario: The assistant will receive customers' names, addresses and order details. The company must keep processing of personal data within the EU.
options: A Global Standard deployment, for the highest quota
OpenAI's public API with an enterprise contract
A Data Zone Standard (EU) deployment in the company's own Foundry resource, called with managed identities
Any deployment, with a system prompt forbidding storage of personal data
questions.explanation: The deployment type decides where requests are processed; Data Zone EU keeps them in the EU, and Azure's terms exclude training on your data. A system prompt cannot control where data is processed.

questions.scenario: Product descriptions are generated with the flagship model. A small model scores 4.4 against the flagship's 4.5 on the evaluation set, at a tenth of the price.
options: Keep the flagship; quality always wins
Fine-tune the flagship to reduce its cost
Switch to a reasoning model
Switch to the small model if 4.4 meets the agreed bar, on a Batch deployment, with human approval of descriptions continuing
questions.explanation: The rule is the smallest model that passes the evaluation, and a bar agreed in advance turns the choice into a decision rather than an opinion. Batch pricing suits work that can wait.

questions.scenario: Ana wants the assistant to know current prices, stock and policies, and proposes fine-tuning monthly.
options: Retrieval: index products and policies in AI Search, retrieve the relevant passages per question, and answer only from them with citations
Fine-tune weekly instead of monthly
Put the whole catalogue in every prompt
Use a larger model that remembers more
questions.explanation: Facts change; retrieval is always current and checkable, while fine-tuned facts go stale and are still hallucinated. Stuffing the catalogue into every prompt is expensive and hurts quality.

questions.scenario: Dev load testing slowed production, although dev and prod have separate Foundry resources in the same subscription and region.
questions.stem: Why, and what is the fix?
options: Separate resources always share models; merge them
Tokens-per-minute quota is per subscription, region and model, so both drew from one pool; put each environment in its own subscription
The playground was open; close it
Dev used a hub; switch to a project
questions.explanation: Quota belongs to the subscription and region, not the resource. Separate subscriptions per environment, as the landing zone intends, keep dev experiments from consuming production capacity.

questions.scenario: The assistant's quality dropped after someone improved the system prompt in the playground and pasted it into production configuration.
questions.stem: Which practice would have caught it?
options: Locking the playground
Keeping the prompt in the repository, changing it by pull request, and running the evaluation set in the pipeline so a lower score fails the build
Asking two people to read the new prompt
Changing prompts only on Mondays
questions.explanation: A prompt is code: versioned, reviewed and gated by tests. Reading a prompt cannot predict its effect across hundreds of questions; an evaluation run can.

questions.scenario: The warehouse wants delivery notes from five large suppliers read automatically, and offline operation when the link drops.
options: A flagship vision model called from the warehouse
Content Understanding in the cloud only
Staff photograph notes and paste them into a chatbot
Custom Document Intelligence models trained on each supplier's layout, run in a container on the warehouse server, with low-confidence fields sent for review
questions.explanation: Fixed layouts suit custom extraction models, which keep field-level confidence for thresholds and review. Containers keep working offline. A flagship model costs more, gives no field confidence and needs the internet.

questions.scenario: RAG answers are often wrong. The right passage appears in the top five results for only 60% of test questions.
options: Chunking by headings with metadata, hybrid search with the semantic ranker, and filters - then re-measure retrieval before touching the prompt
A stronger system prompt
A bigger chat model
More chunks in every prompt
questions.explanation: If the answer is not retrieved, nothing downstream can fix it. Retrieval improvements are measurable against the test set and usually move answer quality most.

questions.scenario: An internal staff assistant uses the same index as the public one. It holds HR guidance only managers may see.
questions.stem: How do you enforce who sees what?
options: Tell the model which users are managers
Build a separate model for managers
Store the allowed groups on each chunk and filter every query by the signed-in user's groups
Remove HR content from search
questions.explanation: Security trimming in the index means content the user may not see never reaches the prompt. Prompt instructions can be bypassed; filters cannot.

questions.scenario: An agent that manages returns uses a service identity with write access to all orders. A crafted message makes it start a return on someone else's order.
options: Add a warning to the system prompt
Tool calls carry the signed-in user's identity and the tools enforce authorisation and validate inputs server-side, with approval for costly actions
Switch to a multi-agent design with a security agent
Log the incident and move on
questions.explanation: The model decides but your code acts, and it must act with the user's permissions. Authorisation in the tool holds whatever the model is persuaded to request; a 'security agent' is just another model that can be fooled.

questions.scenario: A single agent with four tools passes the evaluation set. A proposal adds planner, researcher and critic agents to 'improve quality'.
questions.stem: What should you ask for before approving it?
options: Nothing; more agents are more capable
A named problem the split solves, and evaluation evidence that it improves results enough to justify the extra cost and latency
A different framework
A larger context window
questions.explanation: Each agent multiplies model calls, latency and failure points. Splitting is justified by a specific problem - too many tools, different permissions - and by measured gains, not by architecture diagrams.

questions.scenario: The assistant summarises supplier emails for buyers. One email contains hidden text telling the assistant to mark the supplier as approved.
options: Trust the content filter to stop it
Tell the model in the system prompt to ignore instructions in emails, and nothing more
Prompt Shields on documents, emails marked as untrusted data, no tool that can approve suppliers without a person, and output checks
Summarise only emails from known suppliers
questions.explanation: Indirect injection cannot be fully prevented, so defence is layered: detect it, mark untrusted content, keep tools least-privileged, and put a person in front of consequential actions.

questions.scenario: A model version is retiring, and the replacement is ready to deploy.
questions.stem: What must happen before it serves shoppers?
options: The replacement runs against the evaluation set, including adversarial cases, and ships only if quality, groundedness and safety meet the gate
Nothing; a newer model is always better
A week of manual chatting with it
Deploy it and watch thumbs-down feedback
questions.explanation: A new model changes behaviour in ways no one can predict, so it goes through the same gate as a prompt change. Waiting for feedback lets users find the regressions.

questions.scenario: The monthly AI bill has quadrupled. Five apps call models directly, each with its own key.
questions.stem: What is the most effective first step?
options: Cut every app's quota by 75%
Switch everything to the smallest model
Ban new AI features until next quarter
Put an AI gateway in front of every model call, with managed identities, token limits and token metrics per app, so cost per conversation is visible and controllable
questions.explanation: Without per-app metering nobody knows which app or feature drives the cost. The gateway adds limits, metrics, caching and failover in one place and removes keys from apps; then the right levers can be pulled per app.
